query: When a server answers with HTTP 429, what should the response include?

passages.heading: RFC 6585, section 4 (429 Too Many Requests)
passages.text:
The 429 status code indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time ("rate limiting").

The response representations SHOULD include details explaining the condition, and MAY include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait before making a new request.

query: Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and when can a client retry a request automatically?

passages.heading: RFC 9110, section 9.2.2 (Idempotent Methods)
passages.text:
A request method is considered "idempotent" if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests with that method is the same as the effect for a single such request. Of the request methods defined by this specification, PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent.

Idempotent methods are distinguished because the request can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs before the client is able to read the server's response.

A client SHOULD NOT automatically retry a request with a non-idempotent method unless it has some means to know that the request semantics are actually idempotent, regardless of the method, or some means to detect that the original request was never applied.

query: If a server returns 301 for a POST request, can the browser switch to GET, and how do you prevent that?

passages.heading: RFC 9110, section 15.4.2 (301 Moved Permanently)
passages.text:
The 301 (Moved Permanently) status code indicates that the target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI and any future references to this resource ought to use one of the enclosed URIs.

For historical reasons, a user agent MAY change the request method from POST to GET for the subsequent request. If this behavior is undesired, the 308 (Permanent Redirect) status code can be used instead.

query: A cookie has both Max-Age and Expires. Which one decides when it expires?

passages.heading: RFC 6265, section 4.1.2.2 (The Max-Age Attribute)
passages.text:
The Max-Age attribute indicates the maximum lifetime of the cookie, represented as the number of seconds until the cookie expires. The user agent is not required to retain the cookie for the specified duration.

If a cookie has both the Max-Age and the Expires attribute, the Max-Age attribute has precedence and controls the expiration date of the cookie. If a cookie has neither the Max-Age nor the Expires attribute, the user agent will retain the cookie until "the current session is over" (as defined by the user agent).

query: Do WebSocket frames have to be masked, and in which direction?

passages.heading: RFC 6455, section 5.1 (Overview)
passages.text: To avoid confusing network intermediaries (such as intercepting proxies) and for security reasons that are further discussed in Section 10.3, a client MUST mask all frames that it sends to the server (see Section 5.3 for further details). (Note that masking is done whether or not the WebSocket Protocol is running over TLS.) The server MUST close the connection upon receiving a frame that is not masked. In this case, a server MAY send a Close frame with a status code of 1002 (protocol error) as defined in Section 7.4.1. A server MUST NOT mask any frames that it sends to the client. A client MUST close a connection if it detects a masked frame.

query: How should a JWT's exp claim be checked, and is any clock skew allowed?

passages.heading: RFC 7519, section 4.1.4 ("exp" (Expiration Time) Claim)
passages.text:
The "exp" (expiration time) claim identifies the expiration time on or after which the JWT MUST NOT be accepted for processing. The processing of the "exp" claim requires that the current date/time MUST be before the expiration date/time listed in the "exp" claim.

Implementers MAY provide for some small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes, to account for clock skew. Its value MUST be a number containing a NumericDate value. Use of this claim is OPTIONAL.

query: Is TLS 1.3 0-RTT early data protected against replay?

passages.heading: RFC 8446, section 2.3 (0-RTT Data)
passages.text:
When clients and servers share a PSK (either obtained externally or via a previous handshake), TLS 1.3 allows clients to send data on the first flight ("early data"). The client uses the PSK to authenticate the server and to encrypt the early data.

IMPORTANT NOTE: The security properties for 0-RTT data are weaker than those for other kinds of TLS data. Specifically:

1. This data is not forward secret, as it is encrypted solely under keys derived using the offered PSK.

2. There are no guarantees of non-replay between connections. Protection against replay for ordinary TLS 1.3 1-RTT data is provided via the server's Random value, but 0-RTT data does not depend on the ServerHello and therefore has weaker guarantees.

0-RTT data cannot be duplicated within a connection (i.e., the server will not process the same data twice for the same connection), and an attacker will not be able to make 0-RTT data appear to be 1-RTT data (because it is protected with different keys).

query: What is the difference between the Cache-Control directives no-cache and no-store?

passages.heading: RFC 9111, section 5.2.2.4 (no-cache)
passages.text: The no-cache response directive, in its unqualified form (without an argument), indicates that the response MUST NOT be used to satisfy any other request without forwarding it for validation and receiving a successful response; see Section 4.3.

passages.heading: RFC 9111, section 5.2.2.5 (no-store)
passages.text: The no-store response directive indicates that a cache MUST NOT store any part of either the immediate request or the response and MUST NOT use the response to satisfy any other request.

query: What is the maximum length of a table name in PostgreSQL?

passages.heading: PostgreSQL 17 documentation, 4.1.1 Identifiers and Key Words
passages.text: The system uses no more than NAMEDATALEN-1 bytes of an identifier; longer names can be written in commands, but they will be truncated. By default, NAMEDATALEN is 64 so the maximum identifier length is 63 bytes. If this limit is problematic, it can be raised by changing the NAMEDATALEN constant in src/include/pg_config_manual.h.

query: Does VACUUM FULL in PostgreSQL block other sessions from using the table?

passages.heading: PostgreSQL 17 documentation, VACUUM, parameter FULL
passages.text: Selects “full” vacuum, which can reclaim more space, but takes much longer and exclusively locks the table. This method also requires extra disk space, since it writes a new copy of the table and doesn't release the old copy until the operation is complete. Usually this should only be used when a significant amount of space needs to be reclaimed from within the table.

query: What isolation level does PostgreSQL use by default, and does it support Read Uncommitted?

passages.heading: PostgreSQL 17 documentation, 13.2 Transaction Isolation
passages.text: In PostgreSQL, you can request any of the four standard transaction isolation levels, but internally only three distinct isolation levels are implemented, i.e., PostgreSQL's Read Uncommitted mode behaves like Read Committed. This is because it is the only sensible way to map the standard isolation levels to PostgreSQL's multiversion concurrency control architecture.

passages.heading: PostgreSQL 17 documentation, 13.2.1 Read Committed Isolation Level
passages.text: Read Committed is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL. When a transaction uses this isolation level, a SELECT query (without a FOR UPDATE/SHARE clause) sees only data committed before the query began; it never sees either uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during the query's execution.

query: Can I run CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction in PostgreSQL, and what does it avoid?

passages.heading: PostgreSQL 17 documentation, CREATE INDEX, parameter CONCURRENTLY
passages.text: When this option is used, PostgreSQL will build the index without taking any locks that prevent concurrent inserts, updates, or deletes on the table; whereas a standard index build locks out writes (but not reads) on the table until it's done.

passages.heading: PostgreSQL 17 documentation, CREATE INDEX, Building Indexes Concurrently
passages.text: Another difference is that a regular CREATE INDEX command can be performed within a transaction block, but CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot.

query: Can a PostgreSQL column with a UNIQUE constraint hold more than one NULL?

passages.heading: PostgreSQL 17 documentation, 5.5.3 Unique Constraints
passages.text: In general, a unique constraint is violated if there is more than one row in the table where the values of all of the columns included in the constraint are equal. By default, two null values are not considered equal in this comparison. That means even in the presence of a unique constraint it is possible to store duplicate rows that contain a null value in at least one of the constrained columns. This behavior can be changed by adding the clause NULLS NOT DISTINCT

query: How many columns can a SQLite table have?

passages.heading: SQLite, Limits In SQLite, 3. Maximum Number Of Columns
passages.text: The default setting for SQLITE_MAX_COLUMN is 2000. You can change it at compile time to values as large as 32767. On the other hand, many experienced database designers will argue that a well-normalized database will never need more than 100 columns in a table.

query: Can I use SQLite in WAL mode on a network file share?

passages.heading: SQLite, Write-Ahead Logging, 2. How WAL Works (disadvantages)
passages.text: All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem. This is because WAL requires all processes to share a small amount of memory and processes on separate host machines obviously cannot share memory with each other.

query: Are foreign keys enforced in SQLite by default?

passages.heading: SQLite, Foreign Key Support, 2. Enabling Foreign Key Support
passages.text: Foreign key constraints are disabled by default (for backwards compatibility), so must be enabled separately for each database connection.

query: Does a Python dict keep insertion order, and since which version is that guaranteed?

passages.heading: Python 3 documentation, Built-in Types, Mapping Types — dict
passages.text: Changed in version 3.7: Dictionary order is guaranteed to be insertion order. This behavior was an implementation detail of CPython from 3.6.

query: Why does a Python function with a list as a default argument keep values between calls?

passages.heading: Python 3 documentation, Language Reference, 8.7 Function definitions
passages.text: Default parameter values are evaluated from left to right when the function definition is executed. This means that the expression is evaluated once, when the function is defined, and that the same “pre-computed” value is used for each call. This is especially important to understand when a default parameter value is a mutable object, such as a list or a dictionary: if the function modifies the object (e.g. by appending an item to a list), the default parameter value is in effect modified. This is generally not what was intended. A way around this is to use None as the default, and explicitly test for it in the body of the function

query: What does round(2.5) return in Python?

passages.heading: Python 3 documentation, Built-in Functions, round()
passages.text: For the built-in types supporting round(), values are rounded to the closest multiple of 10 to the power minus ndigits; if two multiples are equally close, rounding is done toward the even choice (so, for example, both round(0.5) and round(-0.5) are 0, and round(1.5) is 2). Any integer value is valid for ndigits (positive, zero, or negative). The return value is an integer if ndigits is omitted or None.

query: Does Python's json.dumps reject NaN values?

passages.heading: Python 3 documentation, json, json.dump() parameter allow_nan
passages.text: allow_nan (bool) – If False, serialization of out-of-range float values (nan, inf, -inf) will result in a ValueError, in strict compliance with the JSON specification. If True (the default), their JavaScript equivalents (NaN, Infinity, -Infinity) are used.

query: What is the largest integer JavaScript can represent exactly?

passages.heading: MDN Web Docs, Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
passages.text:
The Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER static data property represents the maximum safe integer in JavaScript (2^53 – 1).

Double precision floating point format only has 52 bits to represent the mantissa, so it can only safely represent integers between -(2^53 – 1) and 2^53 – 1. "Safe" in this context refers to the ability to represent integers exactly and to compare them correctly. For example, Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 === Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2 will evaluate to true, which is mathematically incorrect.

query: What happens in Go if you write to a nil map?

passages.heading: The Go Programming Language Specification, Map types
passages.text: A nil map is equivalent to an empty map except that no elements may be added.

passages.heading: The Go Programming Language Specification, Index expressions
passages.text: Assigning to an element of a nil map causes a run-time panic.

query: Is the iteration order of a Go map in a for range loop stable?

passages.heading: The Go Programming Language Specification, For statements with range clause
passages.text: The iteration order over maps is not specified and is not guaranteed to be the same from one iteration to the next. If a map entry that has not yet been reached is removed during iteration, the corresponding iteration value will not be produced. If a map entry is created during iteration, that entry may be produced during the iteration or may be skipped.

query: What happens on integer overflow in Rust?

passages.heading: The Rust Programming Language, 3.2 Data Types, Integer Overflow
passages.text:
When you’re compiling in debug mode, Rust includes checks for integer overflow that cause your program to panic at runtime if this behavior occurs.

When you’re compiling in release mode with the --release flag, Rust does not include checks for integer overflow that cause panics. Instead, if overflow occurs, Rust performs two’s complement wrapping. In short, values greater than the maximum value the type can hold “wrap around” to the minimum of the values the type can hold. In the case of a u8, the value 256 becomes 0, the value 257 becomes 1, and so on. The program won’t panic, but the variable will have a value that probably isn’t what you were expecting it to have. Relying on integer overflow’s wrapping behavior is considered an error.

query: What happens when a Kubernetes readiness probe fails, compared with a liveness probe?

passages.heading: Kubernetes documentation, Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes, Liveness probe
passages.text: If a container fails its liveness probe more times than the configured tolerance, the kubelet restarts that container. Liveness probes do not wait for readiness probes to succeed.

passages.heading: Kubernetes documentation, Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes, Readiness probe
passages.text: If the readiness probe returns a failed state, the EndpointSlice controller removes the Pod's IP address from the EndpointSlices of all Services that match the Pod.

query: What is the default restart policy of a Kubernetes Pod?

passages.heading: Kubernetes documentation, Pod Lifecycle, Container restart policy
passages.text: The spec of a Pod has a restartPolicy field with possible values Always, OnFailure, and Never. The default value is Always.

query: In Kubernetes, what happens when a container goes over its CPU limit, and over its memory limit?

passages.heading: Kubernetes documentation, Resource Management for Pods and Containers, How Kubernetes applies resource requests and limits
passages.text:
cpu limits are enforced by CPU throttling. When a container approaches its cpu limit, the kernel will restrict access to the CPU corresponding to the container's limit. Thus, a cpu limit is a hard limit the kernel enforces. Containers may not use more CPU than is specified in their cpu limit.

memory limits are enforced by the kernel with out of memory (OOM) kills. When a container uses more than its memory limit, the kernel may terminate it. However, terminations only happen when the kernel detects memory pressure. Thus, a container that over allocates memory may not be immediately killed. This means memory limits are enforced reactively. A container may use more memory than its memory limit, but if it does, it may get killed.

query: What are the default rolling update settings of a Kubernetes Deployment?

passages.heading: Kubernetes documentation, Deployments, Max Unavailable
passages.text: .spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable is an optional field that specifies the maximum number of Pods that can be unavailable during the update process. The value can be an absolute number (for example, 5) or a percentage of desired Pods (for example, 10%). The absolute number is calculated from percentage by rounding down. The value cannot be 0 if .spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge is 0. The default value is 25%.

passages.heading: Kubernetes documentation, Deployments, Max Surge
passages.text: .spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge is an optional field that specifies the maximum number of Pods that can be created over the desired number of Pods. The value can be an absolute number (for example, 5) or a percentage of desired Pods (for example, 10%). The value cannot be 0 if maxUnavailable is 0. The absolute number is calculated from the percentage by rounding up. The default value is 25%.

query: What happens if a Dockerfile has two CMD instructions?

passages.heading: Docker documentation, Dockerfile reference, CMD
passages.text: There can only be one CMD instruction in a Dockerfile. If you list more than one CMD, only the last one takes effect.

query: How is git push --force-with-lease safer than --force?

passages.heading: Git documentation, git-push, --force-with-lease
passages.text:
Imagine that you have to rebase what you have already published. You will have to bypass the "must fast-forward" rule in order to replace the history you originally published with the rebased history. If somebody else built on top of your original history while you are rebasing, the tip of the branch at the remote may advance with their commit, and blindly pushing with --force will lose their work.

--force-with-lease alone, without specifying the details, will protect all remote refs that are going to be updated by requiring their current value to be the same as the remote-tracking branch we have for them.

query: What does a 0.y.z version mean in Semantic Versioning, and when must the major version go up?

passages.heading: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0, item 4
passages.text: Major version zero (0.y.z) is for initial development. Anything MAY change at any time. The public API SHOULD NOT be considered stable.

passages.heading: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0, item 8
passages.text: Major version X (X.y.z | X > 0) MUST be incremented if any backward incompatible changes are introduced to the public API. It MAY also include minor and patch level changes. Patch and minor versions MUST be reset to 0 when major version is incremented.

query: Can a Prometheus counter go down?

passages.heading: Prometheus documentation, Metric types, Counter
passages.text:
A counter is a cumulative metric that represents a single monotonically increasing counter whose value can only increase or be reset to zero on restart. For example, you can use a counter to represent the number of requests served, tasks completed, or errors.

Do not use a counter to expose a value that can decrease. For example, do not use a counter for the number of currently running processes; instead use a gauge.

query: What does calling model.eval() do in PyTorch?

passages.heading: PyTorch 2.7 documentation, torch.nn.Module.eval()
passages.text:
Set the module in evaluation mode.

This has an effect only on certain modules. See the documentation of particular modules for details of their behaviors in training/evaluation mode, i.e. whether they are affected, e.g. Dropout, BatchNorm, etc.

This is equivalent with self.train(False).

passages.heading: PyTorch 2.7 documentation, torch.optim.Optimizer.zero_grad
passages.text:
Optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)

set_to_none (bool) – instead of setting to zero, set the grads to None. This will in general have lower memory footprint, and can modestly improve performance. However, it changes certain behaviors.

query: Should I apply softmax to the model output before nn.CrossEntropyLoss?

passages.heading: PyTorch 2.7 documentation, torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss
passages.text: The input is expected to contain the unnormalized logits for each class (which do not need to be positive or sum to 1, in general).

query: If I fix the random seed, are PyTorch results reproducible across CPU and GPU?

passages.heading: PyTorch 2.7 documentation, Reproducibility
passages.text: Completely reproducible results are not guaranteed across PyTorch releases, individual commits, or different platforms. Furthermore, results may not be reproducible between CPU and GPU executions, even when using identical seeds.

query: What share of the data goes to the test set in scikit-learn's train_test_split by default?

passages.heading: scikit-learn documentation, sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split, parameter test_size
passages.text: If float, should be between 0.0 and 1.0 and represent the proportion of the dataset to include in the test split. If int, represents the absolute number of test samples. If None, the value is set to the complement of the train size. If train_size is also None, it will be set to 0.25.

query: What regularisation does scikit-learn's LogisticRegression use by default?

passages.heading: scikit-learn documentation, sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression, parameter penalty
passages.text:
'l2': add an L2 penalty term and it is the default choice;

Deprecated since version 1.8: penalty was deprecated in version 1.8 and will be removed in 1.10. Use l1_ratio and C instead.

passages.heading: scikit-learn documentation, sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression, parameter C
passages.text: Inverse of regularization strength; must be a positive float. Like in support vector machines, smaller values specify stronger regularization. C=np.inf results in unpenalized logistic regression.

query: What divisor does numpy.std use by default?

passages.heading: NumPy documentation, numpy.std, parameter ddof
passages.text: Means Delta Degrees of Freedom. The divisor used in calculations is N - ddof, where N represents the number of elements. By default ddof is zero.

query: What does pandas DataFrame.std divide by by default?

passages.heading: pandas documentation, pandas.DataFrame.std
passages.text: Normalized by N-1 by default. This can be changed using the ddof argument.

passages.heading: pandas documentation, pandas.DataFrame.std, parameter ddof
passages.text: Delta Degrees of Freedom. The divisor used in calculations is N - ddof, where N represents the number of elements.
